_about: TEACHING data for Module 1. The protein is the real COX-2 structure 3LN1 (data/docking/cox2.json). Docking poses, scores and compounds A, B and C are MOCK: no docking was run.

purposes.text: Find likely hits in a big compound library (virtual screening)
Predict the binding pose and guide chemical changes (structure-based design)
Explain why similar compounds have different activity (SAR)
Test an existing drug against a new target (repurposing)
Prove that a compound is a drug

scenarios.text: A lab has 2 million commercial compounds for a target enzyme, but the budget lets it test only 50.
scenarios.why: Docking is fast enough to rank a huge library, so it picks the few worth testing.

scenarios.text: You have a hit compound and an X-ray structure. Where does it sit in the pocket and which group should be changed to bind better?
scenarios.why: The predicted pose shows which groups contact the protein and which point into empty space.

scenarios.text: Three analogues were measured in the lab. One is 100 times weaker and nobody knows why.
scenarios.why: Docking each analogue can reveal a lost hydrogen bond or a clash that explains the activity difference.

scenarios.text: An approved drug for one disease might also block a protein linked to a different disease.
scenarios.why: Docking known drugs into a new target is a quick way to suggest repurposing ideas to test.

workflow.q: What are we docking into what, and why?
Is the structure chemically sensible (hydrogens, charges, water)?
Which poses fit best, and how strongly?
Can the protocol reproduce a known answer?
Do the poses and interactions make sense?
What do we take to the lab, and why?

prepare.item: Four copies of the protein (chains A, B, C and D) in the file
prepare.detail: The crystal contains two COX-2 dimers; each copy has its own celecoxib.
prepare.why: Keep one chain (here chain A) and delete the others. Docking into one active site is enough, and extra copies only confuse the setup.
prepare.bad: Extra chains can capture ligands in the wrong place and slow every run.

prepare.detail: More than a hundred water molecules appear in the file, some near the pocket.
prepare.why: Most crystal waters are removed so the ligand can occupy the pocket. Only a few conserved waters that bridge the ligand to the protein are ever kept, and that needs good evidence.
prepare.bad: Leaving all waters in blocks space and can push the ligand into wrong poses.

prepare.item: Celecoxib (CEL) sitting in the active site
prepare.detail: The structure was solved with the drug bound.
prepare.why: Remove it from the receptor, but save a copy: you will re-dock it later to validate the protocol.
prepare.bad: If it stays, it fills the pocket and new ligands have nowhere to go. If you delete it without saving it, you cannot validate.

prepare.detail: COX-2 is a haem-containing enzyme. The haem is deeper in the protein, next to the active site.
prepare.why: A cofactor that belongs to the enzyme is kept. It shapes the protein and the nearby site, so removing it would change the structure you are docking into.
prepare.bad: Removing the cofactor changes the shape and charge of the enzyme.

prepare.item: Sugar chains (NAG) on the protein surface
prepare.detail: N-acetylglucosamine groups are attached to asparagine residues far from the pocket.
prepare.why: They are far from the binding site and not needed for docking. Removing them keeps the system simple.
prepare.bad: Extra groups far away add atoms to every calculation without helping.

prepare.detail: Used to keep the protein soluble in the crystal.
prepare.why: Detergents and other crystallisation additives are artefacts and are removed.
prepare.bad: It is not part of the real system and can cause false interactions.

prepare.detail: X-ray structures usually do not show hydrogens, so the file has none.
prepare.why: Add hydrogens. Hydrogen bonds and charges cannot be scored correctly without them.
prepare.bad: Missing hydrogens mean hydrogen bonds are missed or mis-scored.

prepare.item: Protonation states of His, Asp, Glu (for example His90)
prepare.detail: The charge state of these residues has not been assigned.
prepare.why: Assign protonation states at the relevant pH (often about 7.4). Charge decides whether a residue can donate or accept a hydrogen bond.
prepare.bad: A wrongly charged residue can create or destroy key interactions.

prepare.item: Missing residues and atoms (the file lists residues 570 to 578 as not seen)
prepare.detail: Some parts of the chain were not visible in the crystal.
prepare.why: Check the header (REMARK 465 and 470) for what is missing, and repair or model residues that are near the pocket. Gaps far from the site usually do not matter.
prepare.bad: Gaps near the pocket leave artificial empty space that ligands can wrongly use.

prepare.item: The ligand file is flat (2D) and has no charges
prepare.detail: It was drawn in a sketching tool.
prepare.why: Prepare the ligand: generate 3D coordinates, set protonation and charges for the pH, and minimise. Define rotatable bonds so the program can flex it.
prepare.bad: A flat, uncharged ligand cannot be scored or flexed properly.

terms.label: Hydrogen bond between the sulfonamide and His90
terms.desc: A good donor and acceptor pair at the right distance and angle.

terms.label: Hydrogen bond to Gln192
terms.desc: A second hydrogen bond adds binding energy.

terms.label: Tolyl and CF₃ groups buried in the hydrophobic channel (Val349, Leu352, Phe518, Val523)
terms.desc: Hiding a hydrophobic group from water is a strong driving force.

terms.label: Charged group forms a salt bridge with Arg120 at the channel entrance
terms.desc: Opposite charges attract. Arg120 is where many acidic NSAIDs anchor.

terms.label: Cost of removing water from a charged group (desolvation)
terms.desc: Stripping water from a charged group costs energy, so a salt bridge is never completely free.

terms.label: Steric clash with Phe518
terms.desc: Atoms too close together repel strongly.

validate._about: Mock poses: rot = [axis x,y,z, degrees] about the ligand centre, t = shift in Å. RMSD is computed from the atoms.

setups.title: Setup A
setups.desc: Hydrogens added, one chain kept, box centred on celecoxib, waters removed, default settings.

setups.title: Setup B
setups.desc: Hydrogens NOT added and the box is too small, so the ligand cannot fully enter.

setups.title: Setup C
setups.desc: Setup looks fine, but the scoring function ranks a wrong pose first.

stages.title: Score only
stages.lesson: Most people start here: the most negative score wins. Keep going.

stages.title: Add interactions
stages.lesson: Count hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts. A score without sensible interactions is suspicious.

stages.title: Add key residues
stages.lesson: The reference drug celecoxib binds His90, Gln192 and Arg513 in the selective side pocket of COX-2. A new compound that misses them may not work the same way.

stages.title: Add ligand efficiency
stages.lesson: Ligand efficiency (LE) = -score ÷ heavy atoms. Big molecules score better just by touching more, so LE shows binding per atom.

stages.title: Add pose check
stages.lesson: Is the whole ligand inside the pocket, and does it overlay the reference pose? This catches a good score for a poor pose.

evidence.text: Its docking score (-10.1) is as good as the known reference, celecoxib (-9.6).
It makes the same key hydrogen bonds as celecoxib (His90, Gln192, Arg513).
Its pose overlays the celecoxib pose closely (about 1.2 Å) and sits fully in the pocket.
Its ligand efficiency is similar to celecoxib, so the score is not inflated by size.
It has the most negative docking score of all compounds.
evidence.why: The best score alone is not enough; compound A has it but a poor pose.

evidence.text: It is the largest molecule, so it must bind best.
evidence.why: Size inflates scores. Efficiency and pose matter more.

evidence.text: Docking proves it will be active in cells.
evidence.why: Docking only predicts binding to one target. It cannot prove activity.

nextSteps.text: Check drug-likeness and ADME (can it be absorbed, distributed, metabolised and cleared?).
Test it in a laboratory binding or activity assay.
Check pose stability with a longer simulation (molecular dynamics) if resources allow.
Report it as a confirmed inhibitor.
Skip validation because the score is good.
